title: FOA235 – Business Analytics
text:
1 Welcome
Welcome to the FOA235 course book for HT26.
This book contains the main R code, examples, and practical exercises that we will work with throughout the course. It is intended to support the lectures, labs, and seminars and to serve as a reference when you work independently with R and the course assignments.
Content-wise, the book is aligned with the course textbook, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R, Second Edition. The idea is that you read the course textbook to develop your theoretical understanding and use this compendium as a more practical guide to R code, with examples and exercises that help you apply what you have learned.
It is important to emphasize that there are many ways to write the R code needed to perform the analyses covered in this course. However, throughout the course, we will primarily use the code and approaches presented in this compendium.
The compendium starts with the basics of working with R, RStudio, and Quarto. We then move through descriptive and exploratory data analysis and gradually introduce the modelling process and the three main methods covered in the course:
The course is taught in Swedish, but the compendium is written in English, just like the literature we have in the course.

title: FOA235 – Business Analytics
text:
1.1 R and Posit Cloud
We will use R throughout the course. You do not need any previous experience with R. The first labs introduce R, RStudio, data manipulation, and visualization step by step. We will work in Posit Cloud, which means that you can use RStudio directly in your web browser without installing R on your computer. We will also write all our text and analyses using Quarto in RStudio. In chapter three will we introduce Quarto and explain how we will use it to combine text, R code, results, and figures in a single document.






New to R?



Start with Getting Started with Posit Cloud and then continue with Introduction to R. Next chapter will guide you through how to get started with RStudio in Posit Cloud.

title: FOA235 – Business Analytics
text:
1.2 How to use these materials
The chapters in this guide correspond to different parts of the course. You do not need to read everything at once. Work through the relevant chapters as we progress through the lectures, labs, and seminars.
The practical chapters contain:

explanations,
R code,
examples,
visualizations,
and exercises for you to try yourself.

The book is organized into the following chapters:

Chapter 2: Getting started with Posit Cloud introduces R, RStudio, Posit Cloud, and Quarto.
Chapter 3: Introduction to Quarto documents introduces the type of document we will work with during the course.
Chapter 4: Introduction to coding in R introduces R coding in more detail.
Chapter 5: Introduction to Data Editing introduces data editing.
Chapter 6: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) introduces data preparation, manipulation, visualization, and descriptive analysis.
Chapter 7: Data and Models introduces the modelling process and the three main algorithms used in the course.
Chapter 8: Three Algorithms introduces the three algorithms that we cover during the course.
Chapter 9: Cluster Analysis: Lab 1 introduces Cluster Analysis and the Workflow.
Chapter 10: Cluster Analysis: Lab 2 introduces Multidimensional Cluster Analysis.
Chapter 11: Linear Regression: Lab 1 introduces Supervised Learning and Prediction.
Chapter 12: Linear Regression: Lab 2 introduces Model Selection and Evaluation.
Chapter 13: Logistic Regression: Lab 1 introduces Logistic Regression and Classification.
Chapter 14: Logistic Regression: Lab 2 introduces Model Selection, Validation, and Business Decision.

The chapters are designed to be used alongside the course activities. You do not need to learn all the R code by heart. Instead, focus on understanding what the code does, why we use it, and how the results can help us answer a business or research question.

title: 2  Getting Started with Posit Cloud
text:
2.6 .R files and Quarto files
Two common file types that we use when working with R are .R and .qmd files. An .R file is typically used to write and save R code, while a .qmd file allows us to combine R code with text, figures, tables, and analysis in a single document. This makes your analysis more transparent, easier to share, and above all, reproducible. We will use Quarto documents frequently during the course.
The goal of this course is to introduce analytical thinking and business analytics to business students who are expected to run and lead analytics projects. We believe that to do this effectively, you need hands-on practice and a direct understanding of the workflow that data engineers and analysts use. We believe that working with Quarto documents can help you develop a more efficient and structured workflow by allowing you to combine your code, analysis, results, and written explanations in one place.
A Quarto document should normally be worked through from top to bottom. The order of the code matters because R needs to know about packages, data, and objects before they are used later in the document. For example, a typical Quarto document might follow this order:

Load packages — packages must be loaded before you can use functions from them.
Import data — the data must be loaded into R before you can analyze it.
Create or modify objects — an object must exist before later code can use it.
Analyze the data — for example, calculate descriptive statistics or estimate a model.
Create figures and tables — often using objects or results created earlier.

Think of a Quarto document as a sequence of instructions for R: what happens earlier in the document prepares R for what happens later.

text:
2.9 Installing and loading packages
There is an important difference between installing and loading a package:

Install = make the package available in your Posit Cloud project.
Load = make the package available in your current R session.

A package can also be installed manually using:

install.packages("tidyverse")

Once installed, it can be loaded using:

library(tidyverse)

A useful rule to remember is:

Install when needed → Load each new R session → Use the package’s functions

Try yourself by clicking on the Run Current Chunk button in the upper-right corner of the code chunk you want to run.

2.9.1 Common errors
When you open a course .qmd file, RStudio may detect that the document uses packages that are not yet installed in your Posit Cloud project. If packages are missing, you may see a notification at the top of the Source pane telling you that one or more required packages need to be installed. Use the Install option in this notification to install the required packages. Wait until the installation has finished before running the rest of the document.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.1 Open your Posit Cloud project
Quarto documents allow you to combine text, R code, figures, tables, and results in the same file. The idea is to combine regular text with your code and analysis. This makes it easier for you to both show what you do and describe what you do. You write regular text just like you would in Word — simply type in the white area. Code is written in so-called Executable Cells, or Chunks.
Quarto files use the file extension .qmd.
Follow these steps to create your first Quarto document in Posit Cloud.
Go to: https://posit.cloud
Sign in and open your course project. You should see RStudio running in your browser.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.2 Create a new Quarto document
In RStudio, select:
File → New File → Quarto Document…
A window will appear where you can configure the new document.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.3 Give the document a title
Enter a title for your document, for example:
My Quarto Document
You can also enter your name in the Author field.
Under the output format, select:

Then click Create.

3.4 Install the required packages the first time
The first time you create or render a Quarto document in Posit Cloud, RStudio may tell you that additional packages are required. A message or dialog box may appear asking whether you want to install the required packages. Click Yes to install them. 3.5 Save the document
Select:
File → Save
Give your file a meaningful name, for example:
my_second_quarto_document.qmd
Save the file in the folder: ‘Quarto_files’.
The file extension .qmd tells RStudio that this is a Quarto document. Avoid spaces and special characters in file names. A good convention is to use lowercase letters and underscores.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.6 Look at the Quarto document
At the top of your new document, you will see something similar to:
---
title: "My Second Quarto Document"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---
This is called the YAML header and contains information about the document, such as:
- the title;
- the author;
- and the output format.

To do: Give your document a title and add the author in your Quarto template.

Copy the following code and place it at the very top of your Quarto document.
Change the title, subtitle, author, and select formats: html.



title: "Install R"
subtitle: "R version: "
author: "Niklas Bomark"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%Y-%m-%d')`"
format: html
editor_options:
  chunk_output_type: console

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.7 Add text to your document
A Quarto document can be edited in two different ways: Source mode and Visual mode. Both modes edit the same document—the difference is how you interact with and format the content.
In Source mode, you work directly with the underlying text of the Quarto document. Formatting is created using Markdown syntax. For example, you use # to create a heading and text to make text bold. Source mode gives you direct control over the structure of the document and makes it easy to combine text, Markdown, and R code.
In Visual mode, you work with the document more like you would in Microsoft Word. Instead of writing Markdown syntax yourself, you can use menus and formatting tools to create headings, lists, bold text, links, and other elements. Quarto automatically translates these formatting choices into the underlying Markdown.
You can switch between Source and Visual mode while working on the same document. In this course, it is useful to become familiar with Source mode, since it helps you understand how a Quarto document is structured.
For example, in Source mode you can write:
# Introduction

This is my second Quarto document.
In this document, I will analyze some data using R.
Here, the # tells Quarto that Introduction is a level-one heading. The remaining lines are ordinary body text (paragraphs). You can also create different levels of headings by adding more # symbols:
# Main heading
## Second-level heading
### Third-level heading
This creates a hierarchical structure in your document, similar to using Heading 1, Heading 2, and Heading 3 in Microsoft Word.

To do: Create a heading and some demo text.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.8 Add Code Chunks
Code is written in so-called Executable Cells, or Chunks. An R code chunk looks like this:

1 + 1

[1] 2


You can create a new code chunk by selecting Insert → Executable Cell → R. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Control + E to quickly insert a new R code chunk.

Add a new code cell in your quarto document and type the following code:
example_code <- 1 + 1

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.9 Run the code
You can run a code cell just like you normally run code in R. The easiest way is to click “Run Current Chunk” in the upper right corner of the gray code cell. You can also use the existing keyboard shortcut Control + Shift + Enter (Windows/Linux) or Command + Shift + Enter (Mac) to quickly run all the code in the current gray code cell.
Try running the code cell you just created — it should create an object called example_code with the value 2.
R will execute:

1 + 1

[1] 2


and return:
[1] 2
You can also place the cursor on a line of R code and press:

Windows: Ctrl + Enter
Mac: Cmd + Enter

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.10 Create an object
Let’s create two R objects inside a Code Chunk:

a <- 1
b <- 2

Then use the objects by writing them on the line below (in the same code chunk):

a + b

[1] 3


R should return:
[1] 3
Remember that the order of the code matters. You must create a and b before R can calculate:

text:
3.11 Load packages before using them
If your document uses functions from a package, you first need to load the package. For example, if your function is included in the package called tidyverse, then you first need to load the package (and install it if you didn’t install it via install.packages(“tidyverse”).

library(tidyverse)

✔ dplyr     1.2.0     ✔ readr     2.1.5
✔ forcats   1.0.0     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.2     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.4     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.1     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors


This code must be run before you use functions from the package later in the document. If the package has not been installed, Posit Cloud may show a notification asking you to install it.
A useful rule is:

Install when needed → Load at the beginning of the R session → Use the package

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.12 Datasets for labs
We will work with different datasets throughout the course. Some datasets are located in the project folder that you set up when creating your R project. Other datasets come from the course textbook, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R, and can be accessed by installing and loading the R package ISLR2.

install.packages("ISLR2")
library(ISLR2)

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.13 Work from top to bottom
A Quarto document should normally be worked through from top to bottom. For example:
Load packages
      ↓
Import data
      ↓
Create or modify objects
      ↓
Analyze the data
      ↓
Create tables and figures
      ↓
Interpret the results
Code further down in the document may depend on code that was executed earlier. If you skip an earlier code chunk, R may not know about an object, dataset, or package that you try to use later.

title: 3  Introduction to Quarto documents
text:
3.14 Render the document
When you are ready, click the Render button at the top of the Source pane.
Quarto will:

execute the R code;
generate the results and figures;
combine them with your written text; and
create an HTML document (or a pdf document).

The rendered document will open in a new window or in the Viewer pane.
When you submit your work for INL1, we want you to render and submit a rendered PDF file, together with the Quarto-file. We (teachers) should be able to run the Quarto file and to generate the PDF-file on our own computers.






A good way to work



Do not wait until the end to test your document.
Write a little → run the code → check the result → continue.
This makes it much easier to identify errors and understand what each part of your code does.

title: 4  Introduction to coding in R
text:
4.1 Introduction to coding in R
RStudio is an environment for working with the programming language R. During the course, you will use RStudio to write code, work with data, perform analyses, and create graphs. This guide introduces the most important things you need to know to start coding in R.
We recommend that you read Chapter 2 of An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R while working through this chapter of the compendium. Although the two chapters do not overlap perfectly, some concepts may be easier to understand if you simultaneously apply them in R. For example, when the textbook introduces the concept of a vector, you can directly practice creating and working with vectors in R.
crumbs: 4  Introduction to coding in R

title: 4  Introduction to coding in R
text:
4.1.1 Continue working with my_second_quarto_document
If you do not already have it open, open the file my_second_quarto_document.qmd, located in the Quarto_files folder.
Create a new code chunk and copy-paste the code from the course compendium.

10 - 4

[1] 6

5 * 3

[1] 15

20 / 4

[1] 5

2^3

[1] 8




4.1.2 Creating objects
In R, you can store values in objects. We use the assignment operator <- to store the value on the right in the object on the left. In the example below we store - or assign - the value 10 to the object x. The object x now contains the value 10. You can find all objects under Environment. You can click on them to view more details, or you can refer to them directly in your code. Copy-paste the code into your quarto file.

x <- 10

To see the value, write the object name ‘x’ in a code chunk and press “Run Current Chunk”. You can also write ‘x’ in the Console and press Enter:

x

[1] 10


You can use objects in calculations. For example you can assign 10 to ‘x’ and 5 to ‘y’. Then you can write x + y and R will give you the answer.

x <- 10
y <- 5

x + y

[1] 15


Try it yourself: Create two objects called a and b. Give them any numerical values you want and calculate their sum. You can also type this directly into the Console at the bottom of the screen.


4.1.3 Working with vectors
A vector is a collection of values. The function c() combines values into a vector. In the example below we assign a vector to the new object called ‘ages’.

ages <- c(21, 25, 19, 32, 28)

You can inspect the vector by typing ‘ages’ in a code chunk or in the Console:

ages

[1] 21 25 19 32 28


R contains many useful functions for working with numerical data. Below you find code to calculate the mean and median. The minimal value in a vector, the maximum value in a vector, and the standard deviation of a vector.

mean(ages)

[1] 25

median(ages)

[1] 25

min(ages)

[1] 19

max(ages)

[1] 32

sd(ages)

[1] 5.244044


Try it yourself: Create a vector containing five numbers and calculate its mean and standard deviation.


4.1.4 Functions
A function performs an operation. Functions usually follow this structure:
function_name(argument)
For example:

mean(c(10, 20, 30))

[1] 20


Here: - mean() is the function. - c(10, 20, 30) is the argument supplied to the function.
Some functions have several arguments.For example, the function ‘round’ has two arguments: the number that should be rounded, and to how many digits it should be rounded.

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14




4.1.5 Clearning the working environment
When starting a new project, it’s always a good idea to first clear the R session/environment. You can do this with the following code:

# Clear the environment
rm(list = ls())



4.1.6 Comments
Comments are notes in your code that R does not execute. A comment starts with #.

# Calculate the average
mean(c(10, 20, 30))

[1] 20


Comments are useful for explaining what your code does.


4.1.7 Reading data into R
A common file format is CSV.We will use the readr package to import data. We recommend that you load the data using the code found in the box below. If you have created an R project and saved your data in a folder called Data, it should be enough to just run or copy the code. Double-check that you have a data file in the Data folder. If you don’t, download the data and place it in that folder.

mydata <- read.csv("Data/data_edits.csv")

The data will be stored in an object called mydata. Try yourself: copy the code and paste it into a new code chunk in your R session. Check so that you have a folder called ‘Data’ and a datafile called ‘data_edits.csv’ in the folder.
You can inspect the first five rows with the function head():

head(mydata)

You can also look at the data frame by using the following command:

view(mydata)



4.1.8 Working with a data frame
A data frame is one of the most common ways to store datasets in R. Here is a small example:

students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Anna", "Ben", "Carlos"),
  age = c(22, 25, 21),
  score = c(78, 85, 91)
)

students

    name age score
1   Anna  22    78
2    Ben  25    85
3 Carlos  21    91


You can select one variable using $:

students$score

[1] 78 85 91


You can then calculate, for example, the average score:

mean(students$score)

[1] 84.66667


It is also important to recognize that data can vary in type. A data frame typically contains different types of variables. Here are some common types of variables:
Categorical Variables: Some variables tell us which group or category each individual belongs to. Examples include being male or female, different countries, or telephone area codes (which categorize phone numbers into geographical regions).
Ordinal Variables: A typical course evaluation might ask, “How valuable do you think this course will be to you?” with responses such as: 1 = Worthless; 2 = Slightly; 3 = Middling; 4 = Reasonably; 5 = Invaluable. These categories have a clear order. We also call them factors.
Quantitative Variables: When a variable contains numerical values with meaningful units, we call it a quantitative variable. These variables record an amount or degree of something. For example, degrees Celsius tell us the scale of measurement, so we know how far apart two temperature values are.
Identifier Variables: A variable that has exactly as many unique values as there are cases is called an identifier. These variables uniquely identify each observation, such as student IDs, product IDs, or order numbers.
As you can read in Chapter 2 (pp. 28–29) of An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R, we tend to select statistical learning methods partly based on whether the response variable is quantitative or qualitative.


4.1.9 Creating simple figures/plots
During the course, we will create a lot of figures (often called plots). Later in the course, you will be given code to produce more advanced figures. But we will start simple. Base R can create figures and plots using functions such as hist().

scores <- c(55, 62, 68, 71, 73, 75, 78, 82, 85, 91)

hist(scores)








You will learn more about figures/plots later in the course.


4.1.10 Running several lines of code
You can run one line by placing the cursor on the line and pressing:

Windows: Ctrl + Enter
Mac: Cmd + Enter

You can also select several lines and use the same shortcut to run all selected lines. For example:

x <- 5
y <- 10
z <- x + y

z

[1] 15


It is often useful to run your script from top to bottom. Later lines may depend on objects created earlier in the script.


4.1.11 Reading error messages
Errors are a normal part of programming. For example, this code produces an error because the object does not exist:

my_number + 10

Error: object 'my_number' not found


An error message does not mean that you have failed. It tells you that R could not execute the command.
When you get an error:

Read the error message.
Check the spelling of object and function names.
Check brackets, parentheses, quotation marks, and commas.
Check whether the object you are using has already been created.
Run earlier parts of your script if necessary.



4.1.12 R is case-sensitive
R distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters. These are different object names:

score <- 10
Score <- 20

score

[1] 10

Score

[1] 20


For this reason, be careful with capitalization.

title: 4  Introduction to coding in R
text:
4.2 Good coding habits
A few habits will make working with R much easier:

Write your code in a script rather than only in the Console. Scrips are saved as .r files and looks like a text file. With a script file you will always save your code, and can reproduce your work and analysis.

Give objects clear and meaningful names.
Use comments to explain important steps.
Save your script regularly.
Keep your data files and code organized.
Run your script from top to bottom occasionally to check that everything works.
Read error messages carefully rather than immediately deleting the code.
crumbs: 4  Introduction to coding in R

title: 4  Introduction to coding in R
text:
4.3 Key takeaway
You do not need to memorize every R command. The most important things at the beginning are to understand how to:

write and run code,
create objects,
use functions,
work with files and data,
load packages,
and interpret the output R gives you.

You will become more comfortable with R by using it repeatedly throughout the course.

title: 4  Introduction to coding in R
text:
4.4 Chapter exercise
Create a new Quarto document and complete the following tasks:

Create an object called height and store your height in centimeters.
Create an object called weight and store a weight in kilograms.
Create a vector containing five numerical values.

5.1 Editing Data
In this chapter, we will introduce a few common ways to edit and transform data in R. You can return to this chapter later in the course whenever you need to modify, clean, or restructure your data.
We will begin by adding code to clear the R environment. Clearing the environment removes objects that were created during previous work and gives us a clean starting point. After clearing the environment, you need to load the packages you want to use again with library(). This helps ensure that objects left over from previous analyses do not accidentally interfere with your current work.
We will then import a dataset that we will use throughout the chapter to practice different ways of working with and modifying data.
Open the Lab2.qmd file located in the Lab_files folder. As you work through this chapter in the course compendium, copy the code examples into your Quarto document and run them yourself. title: 5  Introduction to Data Editing
text:
5.1.1 Variable names
Sometimes we need to rename variables. To rename variables, you can use the following principles:

df indicates the object we want to edit.
|> is called a pipe and tells R to continue by adding more operations to the object (in this case, df). You need to have the package dplyr installed and loaded.
The function rename() helps us rename variables. The first argument in rename() is the new name, and the text inside "" after = is the old name.
The function head() tells R that after renaming the variables, we want to display the first six rows of our data frame.

Here is the code:

# Edit and save the new variable names in a new dataset (object) called df_clean
df_clean <- df |> 
  rename(
    age        = "Age..years.", 
    income     = "Income.kr",      
    group      = "Group",          
    codex      = "CodeX",         
    measurement = "Measurement"    
  )  

After running the code, you should see a new object in R — df_clean — and if you click on it, you’ll see the new dataset with the updated variable names. You can also use the function summary() to take a look at the new dataset:

summary(df_clean)

5.1.2 Relevance
Sometimes we have variables that we want to remove from our data frame. The same logic as before applies regarding objects and the pipe operator. What’s new is that we’re using a new function — select() — which we use to choose variables.

# Select variables and save to the df_clean object
df_clean <- df_clean |> 
  select(age, income, region, price, quantity)  # select certain variables

5.1.3 Mutate
The mutate() function from dplyr is used to modify existing variables or to create new variables in a data frame.
Mutate() can be used to modify an existing variable. For example:

df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(
    price = price * 1.10
  )

Here, the existing price variable is replaced with a new version in which all prices have been increased by 10%.
Suppose our dataset contains the variables price and quantity. We can create a new variable called revenue:

df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(
    revenue = price * quantity
  )

The original variables remain in the data frame, and revenue is added as a new variable. We can also create several variables at the same time:

df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(
    revenue = price * quantity,
    revenue_thousands = revenue / 1000
  )

During the course, we will use mutate() when we need to create or transform variables before performing an analysis.


5.1.4 Group
Sometimes we want to calculate statistics for different groups of observations rather than for the entire dataset. For this, we can combine group_by() and summarise() from dplyr.
Suppose our dataset contains a variable called region. We can group the observations by region. By itself, group_by() does not calculate anything. Instead, it tells R that subsequent operations should be performed separately for each group. We can then use summarise() to calculate summary statistics for each group:

df_clean |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    mean_revenues = mean(revenue)
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  region mean_revenues
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 East           3622.
2 North          3072.
3 South          3206.
4 West           3117.


This code can be read as: Take df, then group the observations by region, then calculate the mean of sales separately for each region. We can calculate several statistics at the same time:

df_clean |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_sales = mean(revenue),
    min_sales = min(revenue),
    max_sales = max(revenue)
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  region     n mean_sales min_sales max_sales
  <chr>  <int>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 East      68      3622.     235.      9600.
2 North     61      3072.     162.      9256.
3 South     87      3206.      77.4    10033.
4 West      84      3117.      66.5     9434.


Here: - n() counts the number of observations in each group. - mean() calculates the mean. - min() identifies the minimum value. - max() identifies the maximum value.
The combination of group_by() and summarise() is particularly useful when we want to compare different groups in our data. Note that we don’t ‘save’ the summary statistics we just calculated to a new object



5.1.5 Factors
You always need to be aware of the type of data you are working with. Different data types may need to be handled differently in R. For example, we often need to convert categorical variables into factors. We can do this using the functions mutate() and as.factor().
A factor variable represents data that consist of a set of distinct categories. These categories do not necessarily have a natural order. For example, consider a variable describing the region in which a customer lives:

North
South
West

There is no meaningful ranking among these categories. North is not higher or lower than South or West. This is an example of a nominal categorical variable. In R, we can represent such a variable as an unordered factor.

# Mutate
df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(
    region = factor(
      region,
      levels = c("North", "South", "West"),
      ordered = FALSE
    )
  )

Sometimes, we want to specify an order for the categories of a factor variable. We can do this by setting ordered = TRUE.

5.1.6 Filter
Sometimes we want to edit the rows in our data table. For example, there may be some values that are clearly miscoded. Let’s handle them using a filter with the filter() function. We create a condition — we want to keep only the values that are equal to or greater than 0. Values that are below 0 will simply be removed.

# Filter
df_clean <- df_clean |> 
  filter(price >= 60)     # keep only price values that are 60 or higher

Let’s add a filter that removes all negative values, and another that removes obviously miscoded large values. We use the pipe: |>
This time, we will also save the filtered data to the object ‘df_clean’:

df_clean <- df_clean |> 
  filter(price >= 60) |>        # keep only values that are 60 or higher
  filter(price < 9999999)       # remove extremely large values

We can use filter() when we want to select observations based on their values.



5.1.7 Create new categorical and binary variables
We can also create factors from continuous variables using the functions mutate() and cut(). For example, we can divide the age variable into two groups: younger and older. First, we create the categories and then take a look at the result:

# Example: create categories from a continuous variable
df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(
    age_cat = cut(age,
                  breaks = c(0, 50, Inf),
                  labels = c("Young", "Older"))
  )

We can also create a new variable with two age categories by using a binary numerical indicator variable:

# Example: create a binary numerical variable from a continuous variable
df_clean <- df_clean |>
  mutate(age_binary = ifelse(age > 50, 1, 0))

We often need to handle missing values (NA or missing values). If we look at the data we currently have, we can see that there are some missing values.

title: 6  Describe and Visualize Data
text:
6.2 Univariate Descriptives
Univariate analysis means analyzing one variable at a time. Its important to remember that the type of variable we are working with determines which summary statistics, tables, and plots are appropriate.
For a numerical variable, we are usually interested in:

center,
spread,
shape,
and unusual observations.

For a categorical variable, we are usually interested in:

categories,
frequencies,
and proportions.

Lets go through some code that will do this for us.

6.2.1 Numerical variables
We begin with numerical variables such as age and income.
We can summarize and describe the main characteristics of numerical variables. The following R functions allow us to calculate common measures of center, spread, and range.

# Minimum value: min() returns the smallest value.
min(df_clean$age)

[1] 15

# Maximum value: max() returns the largest value.
max(df_clean$age)

[1] 79

# Range (minimum and maximum): range() returns both the minimum and maximum values.
range(df_clean$age)

[1] 15 79

# Mean: mean() calculates the arithmetic mean (average).
mean(df_clean$age)

[1] 40.7087

# Median: median() returns the middle value when the observations are ordered.
median(df_clean$age)

[1] 40

# Standard deviation: sd() calculates the standard deviation, which describes how spread out the observations are around the mean.
sd(df_clean$age)

[1] 11.478

# Variance: var() calculates the variance, another measure of spread.
var(df_clean$age)

[1] 131.7445

# Quantiles: quantile() returns selected percentiles of the distribution, including the first quartile (25%), median (50%), and third quartile (75%).
quantile(df_clean$age)

  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
  15   33   40   48   79 


We can also use summary() to obtain several important summary statistics at once:

summary(df_clean$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  15.00   33.00   40.00   40.71   48.00   79.00 



6.2.1.1 Missing values
If a variable contains missing values (NA), many of these functions will return NA. We can tell R to ignore missing values by adding na.rm = TRUE:

mean(df_clean$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 40.7087

sd(df_clean$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 11.478

range(df_clean$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 15 79


Here, na.rm = TRUE means remove the NAs before performing the calculation.


6.2.1.2 Histogram
A histogram shows the distribution of a numerical variable. The function we will use in this course requires four arguments: the variable name (including the data frame), the number of bins, the label for the x-axis, and the label for the y-axis.
Let’s try an example by looking at the distribution of age:

histogram(
  df_clean$age,
  bins = 40,
  xlab = "Age",
  ylab = "Frequency",
  suffix = ""
)








When interpreting a histogram, consider the following questions:

Where are most of the observations located?
Is the distribution symmetric or skewed?
Is there one clear peak or several peaks?
Are there any gaps in the distribution?
Are there any unusual or extreme observations?



6.2.1.3 Boxplot for one numerical variable
A boxplot summarizes the center, spread, and potential outliers of a numerical variable. In this course, we will use the following code to produce a simple boxplot for one variable.

boxplot_simple(
  df_clean$income,
  ylab = "Income",
  suffix = "kr"
)








The line inside the box represents the median. The box contains the middle 50% of the observations, from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3). The lines extending from the box are called whiskers, and observations beyond the whiskers are considered potential outliers.
The individual data points are also overlaid on the boxplot, allowing us to see the actual observations behind the summary.
When interpreting a boxplot, consider the following questions:

Where is the median located?
Where are the middle 50% of the observations?
How spread out are the observations?
Does the distribution appear symmetric or skewed?
Are there any potential outliers beyond the whiskers?
If comparing groups, how do their centers, spreads, and outliers differ?




6.2.2 Categorical variables
For categorical variables, we usually examine how observations are distributed across categories. We will use group as an example.

6.2.2.1 Frequency table
A frequency table shows the number of observations in each category.

table(df_clean$region)


North South  West 
   60    87    83 




6.2.2.2 Frequency table with percentages
We can also calculate percentages:

df_clean |>
  count(region) |>
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100
  )

  region  n  percent
1  North 60 26.08696
2  South 87 37.82609
3   West 83 36.08696


This makes it easier to compare the relative size of the categories.


6.2.2.3 Bar chart
A bar chart provides a visual representation of category frequencies.

ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = region)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of observations by group",
    x = "Group",
    y = "Number of observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








When interpreting a bar chart, ask:

Which category is most common?
Which category is least common?
Are observations distributed evenly across categories?

title: 6  Describe and Visualize Data
text:
6.3 Bivariate analysis
Bivariate analysis means examining two variables at the same time. The appropriate method depends on the types of the two variables. Common combinations are:

numerical + numerical,
numerical + categorical,
categorical + categorical


6.3.1 Numerical + numerical
When both variables are numerical, we are often interested in whether they are related.

6.3.1.1 Scatterplot
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables. For example, age and income:

scatterplot(
  df_clean,
  age,
  income,
  xlab = "Age",
  ylab = "Income"
)








When interpreting a scatterplot, ask:

Is there a positive or negative relationship?
Is the relationship approximately linear?
How strong does the relationship appear?
Are there unusual observations?
Are there clusters or other patterns?



6.3.1.2 Correlation
Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two numerical variables. Correlation describes an association. It does not by itself establish direction (causation).

cor(
  df_clean$age,
  df_clean$income,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

[1] -0.05674809


The correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1.

Values close to 1 indicate a strong positive linear relationship.
Values close to -1 indicate a strong negative linear relationship.
Values close to 0 indicate a weak linear relationship.




6.3.2 Numerical + categorical
When one variable is numerical and the other is categorical, we often want to compare the distribution of the numerical variable across groups.

6.3.2.1 Grouped histogram
For example, we can compare income distributions across groups:

histogram_df(
  df_clean,
  xvar = income,
  group_var = region,
  xlab = "Income",
  ylab = "Frequency",
  suffix = " kr",
  bins = 40
)








This allows us to examine whether the groups have different distributions.


6.3.2.2 Boxplot by group
A grouped boxplot is often easier to compare across categories.

boxplot_grouped(
  df_clean$age,
  df_clean$region,
  xlab = "Region",
  ylab = "Age",
  suffix = ""
)








When interpreting the grouped boxplot, compare:

medians,
spread,
potential outliers,
and differences between groups.




6.3.3 Categorical + categorical

6.3.3.1 Cross Table
When both variables are categorical, we can use a cross table.

table(df_clean$age_cat, df_clean$region)

       
        North South West
  Older    13    18   16
  Young    47    69   67


To examine percentages within each age category:

round(prop.table(table(df_clean$age_cat, df_clean$region), margin = 1), 2)

       
        North South West
  Older  0.28  0.38 0.34
  Young  0.26  0.38 0.37

title: 7  Data and Models
text:
7.6 The Modeling Process
How do we go from a business problem to a useful analytical model? In this course, we use CRISP-DM — the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining — as a simple framework for organizing the modeling process.
CRISP-DM divides the process into six phases:

Business Understanding — What problem are we trying to solve? What do we want to know or predict?
Data Understanding — What data do we have? What do the variables represent? Are there obvious patterns or problems?
Data Preparation — Clean, transform, and organize the data so that it can be analyzed.
Modeling — Choose an appropriate method and fit a model to the data.
Evaluation — Assess how well the model works and whether it helps answer the original business question.
Deployment — Use the results, predictions, or model to support decisions or actions.

The process is not strictly linear. For example, while building a model you may discover that a variable needs to be cleaned differently. During evaluation, you may realize that the original business question needs to be refined. You therefore often move back and forth between the different phases.

title: 8  Three Algorithms
text:
8.2 Business applications

8.2.1 K-means cluster analysis
K-means clustering is useful when we want to identify groups of similar observations without having a predefined outcome variable. Examples include:

customer segmentation,
market segmentation,
grouping employees by skill,
grouping products with similar characteristics.

Clustering becomes particularly useful when there are many variables and the groups can no longer be identified by simply looking at a two-dimensional plot.


8.2.2 Multiple linear regression
Multiple linear regression is useful when we want to explain or predict a quantitative outcome using several predictor variables. Examples include:

predicting sales based on marketing expenditure, price, and economic conditions,
estimating customer spending based on demographic and behavioral characteristics,
forecasting employee productivity based on experience, training, and workload,
predicting housing prices based on size, location, and other property characteristics,
estimating production costs based on output, labor, and material inputs.

Regression models can help organizations understand relationships between variables and generate predictions that support planning and decision-making.


8.2.3 Logistic regression
Logistic regression is useful when we want to predict a categorical outcome, most commonly an outcome with two possible classes. Examples include:

predicting whether a customer will make a purchase,
predicting whether a customer will cancel a subscription,
identifying whether a loan applicant is likely to default,
predicting whether an employee will leave the organization,
identifying whether a transaction is potentially fraudulent,
predicting whether a marketing campaign will result in a customer response.

Logistic regression produces estimated probabilities that can be converted into classifications using a chosen classification threshold. This makes the method useful for business decisions where observations need to be assigned to different categories.

title: 8  Three Algorithms
text:
8.3 K-means Cluster Analysis
Cluster analysis is used when we want to discover groups in data. Importantly, the groups are not given to us in advance. The algorithm tries to discover them from patterns in the data. K-means clustering is one of the most widely used clustering algorithms.

8.3.1 A visual starting point
First, clear the Environment and load the required packages:

# Clear the environment
rm(list = ls())

# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
source("Functions/EDA_functions.R")
source("Functions/Cluster_functions.R")
source("Functions/linear_regression_functions.R")
source("Functions/logistics.R")

# Import a dataset
df <- read.csv("Data/df_clean.csv")

Lets plot the relationship between age and income:

scatterplot(
  df,
  age,
  income,
  xlab = "Age",
  ylab = "Income"
)








Look at the relationship between age and income: can you identify groups visually? K-means clustering automates this process. K-means assigns observations to groups based on how similar they are to one another. The basic logic is simple.

8.3.1.1 Step 1: Choose the number of clusters
We decide how many clusters, K, the algorithm should create. For example: K = 3 means that we want the algorithm to create three groups.


8.3.1.2 Step 2: Start with cluster centers
The algorithm selects initial cluster centers, called centroids.


8.3.1.3 Step 3: Assign observations
Each observation is assigned to the closest centroid. The distance between two observations can be calculated using Euclidean distance. For two points, \(p\) and \(q\):
\[
d(p,q) =
\sqrt{
(p_1-q_1)^2 +
(p_2-q_2)^2
}
\]
You do not need to calculate this by hand in this course. R does it for us.


8.3.1.4 Step 4: Update the centers
The centroid of each cluster is recalculated based on the observations currently assigned to that cluster.


8.3.1.5 Step 5: Repeat
The algorithm repeats the assignment and update steps until the clusters stabilize.



8.3.2 Run a simple K-means model
Because K-means clustering is based on distances between observations, variables measured on very different scales should usually be standardized before applying the method. For example, income may be measured in hundreds of thousands of SEK, while age is measured in years. Without standardization, variables with larger numerical values may have a much greater influence on the resulting clusters.
Create a standardized version of the dataset using the code below. You should already be familiar with most of the notation and functions. The new function is scale(), which we use to standardize the variables.

df_km <- df |>
  select(age, income) |>
  na.omit() |>
  scale() |>
  as.data.frame()

Run K-means with three clusters using the following code. The algorithm will: take the standardized data, divide the observations into three clusters, try 25 different starting solutions, keep the best solution, and save the result as an object which we name ‘km’.

set.seed(123)

km <- kmeans(
  df_km,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)

K-means begins by randomly selecting starting positions for the cluster centers. Because of this randomness, running the same analysis twice will produce slightly different results. set.seed(123) makes the random process reproducible. The number 123 itself is arbitrary.
kmeans(…) is the R function that performs K-means clustering.
df_km tells R which data to use. Here, df_km contains the standardized variables age and income.
centers = 3 tells K-means that we want to divide the observations into three clusters.
Because K-means starts from randomly chosen cluster centers, a poor starting point can sometimes produce a poor solution. nstart = 25 tells R to run the K-means algorithm 25 times with different random starting points and keep the best solution.
km <- kmeans stores the result in an object called ‘km’. This object contains information about the clustering, including which cluster each observation belongs to and the location of the three cluster centers.
We also have to add the cluster assignments to the data frame:

df_km$cluster <- factor(km$cluster)

And we can visualize the result:

plot_kmeans_clusters(
  data = df_km,
  var1 = "age",
  var2 = "income",
  kmeans_model = km
)








We now have created groups based on similarities between observations.

title: 8  Three Algorithms
text:
8.4 Linear Regression
Linear regression is used when we want to understand or predict a numerical outcome. Suppose we want to understand whether sales increase when advertising increases. A simple linear regression model can be written as:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \varepsilon
\]
where:

\(y\) is the outcome we want to explain or predict (sales),
\(x\) is a predictor (advertising),
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept,
\(\beta_1\) is the slope,
\(\varepsilon\) represents variation not captured by the model.


Linear regression finds the straight line that best describes the relationship between the variables. We can draw the straight line if we know the intercept and the slope.


8.4.1 A simple linear regression example
Generate a small artificial dataset:

set.seed(123)

df_lm <- tibble(
  advertising = runif(100, 0, 100),
  sales = 100 + 8 * advertising + rnorm(100, 0, 100)
)

Look at the data:

scatterplot(
  data = df_lm,
  xvar = advertising,
  yvar = sales,
  xlab = "Advertising",
  ylab = "Sales"
)








Fit a linear model:

model_lm <- lm(
  sales ~ advertising,
  data = df_lm
)

Visualize the fitted line:

# Visualize the fitted regression model
plot_regression_line(
  data = df_lm,
  model = model_lm,
  xvar = advertising,
  yvar = sales,
  xlab = "Advertising",
  ylab = "Sales"
)








The model simplifies the relationship between advertising and sales into a straight line.
What we have done is that linear regression chooses the values of the model parameters that make the line fit the observed data as closely as possible. The model, in this case, is represented by the intercept and the slope. The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by the model is called a residual.
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) chooses the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals. You do not need to calculate the solution by hand in this course. R estimates the model for us. Later, we will extend this idea to multiple linear regression, where several predictor variables are used together.

title: 8  Three Algorithms
text:
8.5 Logistic Regression
Logistic regression is used when the outcome has two categories. Instead of predicting a numerical value such as sales, logistic regression predicts the probability that an event occurs. For example: What is the probability that a customer makes a purchase?
The predicted probability is always between:
\[
0 \leq P(Y=1) \leq 1
\]

8.5.1 A simple logistic regression example
Generate artificial data where the probability of purchase increases with customer engagement. (You don’t need to understand this code example):

set.seed(123)

n <- 150

df_logit <- tibble(
  engagement = runif(n, 0, 10)
) |>
  mutate(
    probability = plogis(-5 + engagement),
    purchase = rbinom(
      n,
      size = 1,
      prob = probability
    )
  )

Look at the observations:

scatterplot(
  data = df_logit,
  xvar = engagement,
  yvar = purchase,
  xlab = "Customer engagement",
  ylab = "Purchase (0 = No, 1 = Yes)"
)








Fit a logistic regression model:

# Fit the logistic regression model
model_logit <- glm(
  purchase ~ engagement,
  data = df_logit,
  family = binomial
)

Visualize the estimated probability:

# Plot observed outcomes and predicted probabilities
plot_logistic_predictions(
  model = model_logit,
  df = df_logit,
  x_var = "engagement",
  y_var = "purchase",
  title = "A logistic regression model",
  x_label = "Customer engagement",
  y_label = "Probability of purchase"
)








The S-shaped curve represents the model’s estimated probability. As engagement increases, the estimated probability of purchase also increases. Often we want to set some kind of classification threshold. In this case we will set it to 0.5 so that every observation below 0.5 is a ‘No’, and every observation above or equal to 0.5 is a ‘Yes’:

plot_logistic_predictions(
  model = model_logit,
  df = df_logit,
  x_var = "engagement",
  y_var = "purchase",
  threshold = 0.5, # predicted probability
  title = "A logistic regression model",
  x_label = "Customer engagement",
  y_label = "Probability of purchase"
)








You can experiment with different classification thresholds for the predicted probabilities and observe how the resulting classifications change. Later in the course, we will evaluate these classifications by examining how many observations are correctly and incorrectly classified into each category.

  k.max = 10
)








As k increases, the within-cluster variation will decrease. However, at some point, adding another cluster provides only a relatively small improvement. We look for the point where the reduction begins to level off. This is often referred to as the elbow.
Questions:

What happens to the within-cluster sum of squares as k increases?
Where do you see an elbow in the figure?
Based on the elbow method, what value of k would you choose?
Is the choice completely unambiguous?



9.1.3.7 Run K-means
Now use the value of k that you selected. For example, if you selected k = 3, you would run:

set.seed(123)

km <- kmeans(
  cluster_data_scaled,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)

Replace 3 with the value of k that you selected if necessary. Examine the number of observations in each cluster:

table(km$cluster)


 1  2  3 
51 62 67 


Questions:

How many observations were assigned to each cluster?
Are the clusters approximately equal in size?
Would equal cluster sizes necessarily be expected in real data?



9.1.3.8 Visualize the clusters
In this lab, the observations are easy to visualize because the dataset contains only two variables. If the dataset included more than two variables, as in the next lab on K-means Cluster Analysis, we could first apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the data. We could then visualize the observations by plotting their scores on the first two principal components, which capture as much of the variation in the original data as possible.
To simplify our workflow, we will use another R package, called factoextra, to visualize the results of our cluster analysis from this point onward. The package produces clear and informative plots and can also automatically apply PCA before plotting when the dataset contains more than two variables.
Plot our clusters with factoextra:

fviz_cluster(
  km,
  data = cluster_data_scaled,
  geom = "point",
  ellipse.type = "convex",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)








Questions:

Do the resulting clusters correspond to the patterns you observed in the original scatterplot?
Are the clusters clearly separated?
Are there observations close to the boundaries between clusters?
Does the value of k you selected still appear reasonable after inspecting the clustering result?



9.1.3.9 Interpret the clusters
We standardized the variables before running K-means because the algorithm is based on distances between observations. However, for interpretation, it is often more useful to return to the original scale of the variables.
First, add the cluster assignments to the original data:

df$cluster <- factor(km$cluster)

We can then calculate the mean of each original variable for each cluster:

cluster_summary <- df |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_x1 = mean(x1),
    mean_x2 = mean(x2)
  )

cluster_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  cluster     n mean_x1 mean_x2
  <fct>   <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 1          51   1.54    1.15 
2 2          62   0.450  -1.22 
3 3          67  -1.57    0.849


The K-means algorithm was fitted using the standardized data, but the table above describes the resulting clusters using the original values of x1 and x2.
Questions:

How many observations belong to each cluster?
What is the average value of x1 and x2 in each cluster?
How do the clusters differ from one another?
How would you describe each cluster in words based on its original values?

So remember: Standardize for clustering; return to the original scale for interpretation.


9.1.3.10 Should we use the model?
Should we use the model in our firm? Is it a good model? In the next lab we will take what we learned during this lab and place it in the CRISP-process.


9.1.3.11 What have we learned?
In this exercise, the number of clusters was not given to us. Instead, we treated k as a decision that had to be made as part of the analysis.
Our workflow was:

Explore the data.
Select variables for clustering.
Standardize the variables.
Investigate possible values of k.
Choose k.
Run K-means.
Inspect, visualize, and interpret the resulting clusters.

The elbow method can help us choose a reasonable value of k, but it does not always provide one objectively correct answer. Choosing the number of clusters often requires combining statistical tools with visualization and substantive knowledge about the data.


9.1.3.12 A Compact K-means Workflow
When experimenting with different values of \(k\), it is convenient to keep the main steps in one code chunk. Change only the value of number of centers and re-run the chunk. Look at the plot.

set.seed(123)

# 1. Run k-means
km <- kmeans(
  cluster_data_scaled,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)

# 2. Visualize the result
fviz_cluster(
  km,
  data = cluster_data_scaled,
  geom = "point",
  ellipse.type = "convex",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

title: 10  Cluster Analysis: Lab 2
text:
10.1 Multidimensional K-means Cluster Analysis
In this lab, we will import a dataset containing many variables, standardize the variables, and then perform a k-means cluster analysis to explore whether there are distinct groups in the data. Since we are working with multidimensional data, we will use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to visualize the resulting clusters in two dimensions. We will also evaluate the clustering solution using the elbow method. Finally, we will interpret the results and make a decision about whether the chosen clustering model should be implemented in the company.
We will follow this basic workflow when we work with K-Means Cluster Analysis:

title: 10  Cluster Analysis: Lab 2

10.1.1 Learning objectives
After completing this lab, you should be able to:

prepare data for cluster analysis;
standardize variables;
perform a k-means cluster analysis;
use the elbow method to select the number of clusters;
visualize multidimensional clusters using PCA;
evaluate how well-separated the clusters are;
interpret the clusters;
make a recommendation based on the analysis.



10.1.2 Exercise 1: Multidimensional K-means Cluster Analysis

10.1.2.2 Select variables for clustering
K-means clustering is based on numerical distances. We therefore need to select the numeric variables that we want the algorithm to use. Suppose the dataset contains an ID variable called customer_id. We do not want to use the ID when forming clusters.

- Which variables are now included in the cluster analysis?
- Why should an identification number such as customer_id not be included?
- Why does k-means generally require numerical variables?


10.1.2.3 Check missing values
Before running the cluster analysis, check whether the selected variables contain missing values.

10.1.2.4 Examine the variables
Before clustering, inspect the descriptive statistics.

age may range from 18 to 80;

Questions:
- Why could it be problematic to perform k-means clustering directly on variables measured on very different scales?


10.1.2.5 Scaling: Standardize the variables
We standardize the variables. After standardization, each variable has approximately:
- mean = 0;
- standard deviation = 1.

df_scaled <- df_cluster |>
  scale() |>
  as.data.frame()

Inspect the standardized data.

- Why is standardization especially important for k-means clustering?


10.1.2.6 How many clusters should we use?
K-means requires us to choose the number of clusters, (k), before estimating the model. One common method for selecting (k) is the elbow method. The elbow method compares the total within-cluster variation for different values of (k).

set.seed(123)

fviz_nbclust(
  df_scaled,
  kmeans,
  method = "wss",
  k.max = 10
)








The vertical axis shows the within-cluster sum of squares. As the number of clusters increases, the within-cluster variation decreases. However, adding more and more clusters eventually produces only small improvements. We look for an elbow in the plot: a point where adding another cluster produces a much smaller improvement.
Questions:
- Where do you see an elbow in the figure?
- How many clusters would you choose?
- Is the choice completely obvious?


10.1.2.7 Run the k-means model
Suppose that we decide to use three clusters. We set a seed to make the results reproducible.

set.seed(123)

km <- kmeans(
  df_scaled,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)



10.1.2.8 Add cluster membership to the data
Count the observations in each cluster.

table(km$cluster)


  1   2   3 
121 149 130 




10.1.2.9 Examine the cluster centers
The cluster centers help us understand what characterizes each cluster. The centers stored in the k-means model are based on the standardized variables.

km$centers

         age     income annual_spending  purchases website_visits satisfaction
1  1.1018965 -0.1210603      -0.4188867 -0.8491492    -1.15386776   -0.1030609
2 -1.0041921 -0.9288419      -0.7601506 -0.3621093     0.89255368   -0.4788992

- What seems to characterize Cluster 1?
- What seems to characterize Cluster 2?
- What seems to characterize Cluster 3?
- Which variables appear to distinguish the clusters most strongly?


10.1.2.10 Interpret clusters using the original scale
Standardized values are useful for clustering because they ensure that variables measured on different scales contribute more equally to the analysis. However, standardized values can be difficult to interpret. To better understand the clusters, we can therefore calculate the average of each variable on its original scale within each cluster.
For this step, we will introduce two new functions: across() and where(). This is the only time we will use these functions in this lab, so you do not need to understand them in detail. It is enough to copy the code and make the necessary changes to fit your dataset.
First, however, we need to extract the cluster assignments from the K-means model and add them to our original, unscaled data frame:

df_results <- df_cluster |>
  mutate(
    cluster = factor(km$cluster)

Inspect the result.

We can now calculate summary statistics for the variables on their original scale:

cluster_summary <- df_results |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

For example:

“High-value customers”
“Price-sensitive customers”
“Occasional customers”

Your names should be based on the actual characteristics of your clusters.


10.1.2.11 Visualize many variables?
In the first lab on cluster analysis we only had two variables. In this lab we have more. This means that the observations exist in a multidimensional space. To visualize the clusters, we use Principal Component Analysis (PCA). PCA summarizes the variation in many variables using a smaller number of dimensions (in our case: 2!). We will not focus on how to perform PCA or on the mathematical details behind it. However, you should understand the basic idea and purpose of PCA, as this will help you interpret the visualizations we create.
We will use the factoextra package. Here is the code:

fviz_cluster(
  km,
  data = df_scaled,
  geom = "point",
  ellipse.type = "convex",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)








Questions:
- Do the clusters appear clearly separated?
- Is there considerable overlap between any clusters?
- Which clusters appear most similar?
- Does the PCA visualization support the idea that three meaningful clusters exist?


10.1.2.12 Compare alternative models
Suppose you are considering models with 2, 3, and 4 clusters. Run all three models.

set.seed(123)

km2 <- kmeans(
  df_scaled,
  centers = 2,
  nstart = 25
)

km3 <- kmeans(
  df_scaled,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)

km4 <- kmeans(
  df_scaled,
  centers = 4,
  nstart = 25
)

Calculate the total within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) for each model and compare the results.

comparison <- data.frame(
  clusters = c(2, 3, 4),
  WSS = c(
    km2$tot.withinss,
    km3$tot.withinss,
    km4$tot.withinss
  )
)

comparison

  clusters       WSS
1        2 1457.3222
2        3  804.8805
3        4  722.2749


WSS will always decrease as we add more clusters because observations can be grouped into increasingly smaller and more homogeneous clusters. Therefore, we should not simply choose the model with the lowest WSS.
Instead, we should consider how much the WSS decreases when moving from 2 to 3 clusters and from 3 to 4 clusters. If adding another cluster results in only a small additional decrease in WSS, the more complex model may not provide much improvement.
This is the same logic that underlies the elbow method. We can examine the change in WSS explicitly:

comparison <- comparison |>
  mutate(
    WSS_reduction = lag(WSS) - WSS
  )

comparison

  clusters       WSS WSS_reduction
1        2 1457.3222            NA
2        3  804.8805     652.44173
3        4  722.2749      82.60554


Questions:
- How much does WSS decrease when moving from 2 to 3 clusters?
- How much does it decrease when moving from 3 to 4 clusters?
- Which model is easiest to interpret?


10.1.2.13 Business interpretation
Imagine that you work for a company that wants to use the clusters to develop different strategies for different groups of customers. For example, the company could use the clusters for:

targeted marketing;
personalized offers;
customer retention;
pricing strategies;
product recommendations.

Study your cluster summaries again.

  cluster   age income annual_spending purchases website_visits satisfaction
  <fct>   <dbl>  <dbl>           <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>
1 1        60.8 52807.           3055.      13.1           17.1         7.06
2 2        27.8 32735.           2364.      18.3           54.8         6.57
3 3        45.5 85069.           6454.      35.1           39.3         8.03


Questions:
- What practical differences exist between the clusters?
- Could the company realistically use these clusters to make different decisions?
- What strategy would you recommend for each cluster?
- Are the differences between the clusters large enough to justify treating them differently?


10.1.2.14 Implementation decision
You are now responsible for recommending whether the company should implement the clustering model. Consider the following evidence:

the elbow method;
the silhouette analysis;
the PCA visualization;
the size of the clusters;
how distinct the cluster profiles are;
whether the clusters have meaningful business interpretations.



10.1.2.15 Final task
Write a short recommendation to management. Your recommendation should answer the following questions:

How many clusters do you recommend?
What characterizes the clusters?
How well-separated are they?
Are the clusters meaningful from a business perspective?
Should the company implement the clustering model?

Conclude with one of the following recommendations:
Implement the model
or
Do not implement the model
Briefly justify your decision.

title: 11  Linear Regression: Lab 1
text:
11.1 Introduction
In the previous labs, we worked with k-means clustering. K-means is an unsupervised learning method. There is no outcome variable that the model is trying to predict. Instead, the algorithm searches for patterns in the data and groups similar observations together.
We now move to supervised learning. In supervised learning, we have an outcome variable that we want to explain or predict using one or more predictor variables.
In this lab, we will introduce a basic modeling workflow for supervised learning. This workflow differs somewhat from the workflow we used in the previous lab, where we worked with unsupervised learning. We will work with the following overarching steps:
We will begin this workflow using linear regression. In chapter 12 and 13 we will use a similar workflow but with logistic regression.

title: 11  Linear Regression: Lab 1
text:
identify the outcome and predictor variables
split the data into training and test data
fit different models using the training data
compare how well the models fit the training data
select a model
use the selected model to make predictions on the test data
evaluate the model’s predictive performance using the test data



11.1.1 Learning objectives
After completing this lab, you should be able to:

distinguish between outcome and predictor variables
explain the basic idea behind linear regression
fit a simple linear regression model in R
interpret the intercept and slope
calculate predicted values
understand the difference between observed and predicted values
calculate prediction errors
explain why we separate training, and test data



11.1.2 Prepare the R session
We begin by clearing the Environment and loading the packages used in the lab.

# Clear Environment
rm(list = ls())

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

source("Functions/EDA_functions.R")
source("Functions/linear_regression_functions.R")



11.1.3 Import the data
In this lab, imagine that we work for a company that wants to understand and predict sales. The company has collected information about its marketing activities. Lets import some data.

# Import the data
df <- read.csv("Data/regression_data.csv")

Take a first look at the data.

11.1.3.1 Questions

How many observations are in the dataset?
Which variables are included?
Which variable do you think we should try to predict?
Which variable could be used to predict it?
Do you find anything in the data that might be problematic?




11.1.4 Outcome and predictor variables
In supervised learning, we distinguish between outcome variables and predictor variables.

The outcome variable is the variable we want to explain or predict.
The predictor variable contains information that we use to make that prediction.

Suppose we want to predict sales using marketing. In this case:

sales is the outcome variable;
marketing is the predictor variable.

We can write this relationship as:
\[
Sales = f(Marketing)
\]
This simply means that we are interested in whether information about marketing can help us understand or predict sales.


11.1.5 Explore the relationship
Before fitting a model, we should always explore the data. Because both variables are quantitative, a scatter plot is useful.

scatterplot(
  df,
  marketing,
  sales,
  xlab = "Marketing",
  ylab = "Sales"
)









11.1.5.1 Questions

Does there appear to be a relationship between marketing and sales?
Is the relationship positive or negative?
Does the relationship appear approximately linear?




11.1.6 The linear regression model
Linear regression describes the relationship between an outcome variable and one or more predictor variables using a line. For a simple linear regression with one predictor, the fitted model can be written as:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x
\]
where:

\(\hat{y}\) is the predicted value of the outcome
\(b_0\) is the intercept
\(b_1\) is the slope
\(x\) is the predictor variable

For our example:
\[
\widehat{Sales} = b_0 + b_1 Marketing
\]
The model tries to find the line that best represents the relationship between marketing and sales. The position and slope of this line are determined by two coefficients, \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), which are estimated from the data. Together, these coefficients define the best-fitting line—the line that minimizes the squared differences between the observed sales values and the values predicted by the model.


11.1.7 Fit the model
We use the lm() function to estimate a linear regression model.

model <- lm(
  sales ~ marketing,
  data = df
)

View the estimated coefficients.

coef(model)

11.1.8 Interpret the model
Suppose the estimated model is:
\[
\widehat{Sales} = 20 + 2.5 \times Marketing
\]
The intercept of 20 means that the model predicts sales of 20 when marketing is 0. The slope of 2.5 means that a one-unit increase in marketing is associated with an increase of 2.5 units in predicted sales.

We can add the fitted regression line to the scatter plot.

  data = df,

  ylab = "Sales"
)

Does the regression line appear to represent the relationship reasonably well?
Are all observations located exactly on the line?
Why do you think observations differ from the regression line?




11.1.10 Make predictions
Once we have fitted a model, we can use it to make predictions. Suppose marketing is equal to 30.

new_customer <- data.frame(
  marketing = 30
)

predict(
  model,
  newdata = new_customer
)

96.34116

What sales value does the model predict when marketing is: 30, 35, 55?
Use your regression equation to calculate the same prediction by hand.




11.1.11 Predicted values for all observations
We can also calculate a prediction for every observation in the dataset.

df$predicted_sales <- predict(model)

Inspect the results.

head(df)

  marketing sales predicted_sales

the observed value: sales;
the model’s prediction: predicted_sales.



11.1.12 Prediction error
A model will normally not predict every observation perfectly. The difference between the observed value and the predicted value is called a residual or prediction error.
\[
Error = Observed - Predicted
\]
Calculate the errors.

df <- df |>
  mutate(
    error = sales - predicted_sales
  )

Inspect the results.

  marketing sales predicted_sales      error

# Plot the prediction errors
plot_residuals(
  data = df,
  xvar = marketing,
  errorvar = error,
